# Flight of the Night Butterfly

You need to guide a night butterfly through the darkness. Its starting point is the common center of six radial tracks, numbered clockwise from $$$0$$$ to $$$5$$$. Track $$$0$$$ is the main track; the other five are auxiliary tracks.

Only certain intervals on the tracks are lit. The main track has one set of lit intervals, while all five auxiliary tracks share another set. All lit intervals are closed, and their endpoints represent distances from the center.

Before each flight, you may choose a positive real speed $$$d$$$, which remains fixed throughout the flight. The butterfly starts at the center at time $$$0$$$. At every positive integer time $$$t$$$, it is on track $$$(t\bmod 6)$$$ at a distance $$$t\cdot d$$$ from the center. Thus, it visits tracks $$$1,2,3,4,5,0,1,2,\ldots$$$ in this order.

You are given $$$q$$$ queries, each specifying a target distance $$$T$$$. You want the butterfly to reach the main track at some time $$$k$$$, at a distance $$$T$$$ from the center. Thus, $$$k$$$ must be a positive multiple of $$$6$$$, and $$$k\cdot d=T$$$. At every integer time $$$1,2,\ldots,k$$$, the butterfly must be within a lit interval on its current track, or it will fall into darkness and lose its way. There are no restrictions at other times, including time $$$0$$$.

For each query, find the earliest time $$$k$$$ at which the butterfly can safely reach its target, or print `-1` if it cannot. The queries are independent, and you may choose $$$d$$$ separately for each query.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1\le n,m\le50$$$), representing the numbers of lit intervals on the main track and in the set shared by all five auxiliary tracks, respectively.

Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1\le l\le r\le10^{18}$$$), representing a lit interval $$$[l,r]$$$ on the main track.

Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1\le l\le r\le10^{18}$$$), representing a lit interval $$$[l,r]$$$ shared by all five auxiliary tracks.

Within each set, the intervals are pairwise disjoint and are given in increasing order of their left endpoints. In particular, consecutive intervals satisfy $$$l_{i+1} \gt r_i$$$.

The next line contains an integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1\le q\le100$$$), representing the number of queries.

Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le10^{18}$$$), representing the target distance of one query.

## Output

For each query, print on a separate line the earliest time $$$k$$$ at which the butterfly can safely reach its target, or `-1` if it cannot.

## Note

For $$$T=6$$$, choosing $$$d=1$$$ lets the butterfly reach the target at time $$$k=6$$$. The distances at the first five integer times are $$$1,2,3,4,5$$$, all in the lit interval $$$[1,5]$$$ on the auxiliary tracks. At the sixth integer time, the distance is $$$6$$$, which is in the lit interval $$$[6,6]$$$ on the main track.

For $$$T=12$$$, choosing $$$d=1$$$ lets the butterfly reach the target at time $$$k=12$$$. Its distances while on the auxiliary tracks are all in $$$[1,5]\cup[7,11]$$$, while its distances on the main track are $$$6$$$ and $$$12$$$. To arrive at time $$$k=6$$$, it would need $$$d=2$$$, but then at time $$$3$$$ it would be at an unsafe position at distance $$$6$$$ from the center on an auxiliary track.

The diagrams below show the query $$$T=12$$$. The first two use $$$d=1$$$, and the third uses $$$d=2$$$. Gold segments and points are lit intervals. Dark blue dots are labeled with their times, and the red cross marks a position in darkness. The second panel continues from the hollow dot at time $$$6$$$. Dashed arrows show only the order of integer-time positions, not the actual flight path between them.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/c43f23c658b8c505d9c57cfce09608ae98409ed5.png)

For $$$T=18$$$, the target is outside every lit interval on the main track, so it cannot be reached safely.

# Growing Prefix Span

For a permutation of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$, let $$$s_i$$$ be the length of the shortest contiguous subarray containing all values $$$1,2,\ldots,i$$$.

Let $$$\operatorname{pos}_p(x)$$$ be the position of $$$x$$$ in the permutation; we have

$$$$$$ s_i=\max_{1\le x\le i}\operatorname{pos}_p(x)-\min_{1\le x\le i}\operatorname{pos}_p(x)+1. $$$$$$

For each $$$i$$$, an interval constraint $$$[l_i,r_i]$$$ is given.

Please count the permutations satisfying $$$l_i\le s_i\le r_i$$$ for every $$$i$$$. Print the answer modulo $$$998244353$$$.

The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5$$$).

## Output

Print the number of valid permutations modulo $$$998244353$$$.

Please note that a valid permutation may not exist.

The valid permutations in the example are $$$(1,2,3)$$$, $$$(2,1,3)$$$, $$$(3,1,2)$$$, and $$$(3,2,1)$$$.

# Hidden Permutation

This is a communication problem. Your program will be run twice for each test, in two independent processes.

First Run

You are given a permutation $$$p=(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n)$$$ of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$.

Output an $$$n\times n$$$ matrix $$$A$$$ such that each row is a permutation of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$ and all rows are pairwise distinct.

Second Run

Before the second run, the judge randomly shuffles the rows of $$$A$$$ to obtain a matrix $$$B$$$. The order of the elements within each row remains unchanged. You are given $$$B$$$ and must recover the original permutation $$$p$$$ from the first run.

Your program must recover $$$p$$$ for every possible ordering of the rows. No process state is preserved between the two runs; the shuffled matrix is the only information passed from the first run to the second. The time and memory limits apply to each run separately.

## Input

The first line contains a string `op` (either `first` or `second`) and an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$3\le n\le 2000$$$), indicating the run and the size of the permutation. The value of $$$n$$$ is the same in both runs.

If `op` is `first`, the second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n$$$ ($$$1\le p_i\le n$$$), a permutation of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$.

If `op` is `second`, each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains $$$n$$$ integers, describing one row of $$$B$$$. This is the matrix output in the first run with only its rows randomly reordered.

There is one test case per run.

## Output

If `op` is `first`, output $$$n$$$ lines, each containing $$$n$$$ space-separated integers, describing the matrix $$$A$$$. Each row must contain every integer from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ exactly once, and the $$$n$$$ rows must be pairwise distinct.

If `op` is `second`, output $$$n$$$ space-separated integers on one line: the original permutation $$$p$$$ from the first run, in its original order.

## Note

The two examples show the first and second runs of one possible solution on the same test.

In the first run, the input permutation is $$$(2,3,1)$$$, and the program outputs a $$$3\times 3$$$ matrix whose rows are pairwise distinct permutations of $$$1,2,3$$$.

Before the second run, the judge places the third, first, and second rows of this matrix in that order. The elements within each row remain unchanged. From the resulting matrix, the program must recover and output $$$(2,3,1)$$$. The row order used during judging may differ from the example.

# Jobs through Pipelines

You need to schedule $$$n$$$ jobs on a pipeline. The jobs form a sequence, and job $$$i$$$ has workload $$$a_i$$$. The pipeline consists of $$$m$$$ stages in series.

Before processing begins, you may choose an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$0\le t\le n$$$). This moves the first $$$t$$$ jobs to the end without changing their relative order, obtaining $$$a_{t+1},a_{t+2},\ldots,a_n,a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_t.$$$ Choosing $$$t=0$$$ or $$$t=n$$$ leaves the sequence unchanged.

Next, you need to partition the resulting sequence into at most $$$k$$$ nonempty contiguous segments, each forming a batch. The workload of a batch is the sum of the workloads of its jobs.

The batches then enter the pipeline in order. Each batch passes through stages $$$1,2,\ldots,m$$$ in this order, taking time equal to its workload at each stage. Each stage processes at most one batch at a time, following the batches' left-to-right order in the sequence. After finishing at one stage, a batch may wait for the next stage to become available. While it waits, it no longer occupies the previous stage, which may process the next batch. Different stages may process different batches simultaneously.

The pipeline starts processing at time $$$0$$$. Choose the prefix to move and the partition into batches so that all jobs finish as early as possible.

## Input

The first line contains three integers $$$n,m,k$$$ ($$$1\le n,m\le 5\times 10^5$$$, $$$1\le k\le n$$$): the number of jobs, the number of stages, and the maximum number of batches.

The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ ($$$1\le a_i\le 10^6$$$), the workloads of the jobs.

## Output

Print one integer: the minimum possible time at which all jobs have finished.

## Note

An optimal choice is to move the prefix $$$[3,1,4]$$$ to the end, obtaining the sequence $$$[2,3,1,4]$$$, and partition it into two batches $$$[2,3]$$$ and $$$[1,4]$$$. Both batches have workload $$$5$$$. They can start at the first stage at times $$$0$$$ and $$$5$$$, and finish at the third stage at times $$$15$$$ and $$$20$$$, respectively. Thus, all jobs finish at time $$$20$$$, which is the minimum possible time.
content.title: Jobs through Pipelines

# Keep on the Right Track

You enjoy exploring the world by car. Today, you have arrived in a new country consisting of $$$n$$$ cities, numbered $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$.

You wish to drive to the capital city, $$$t$$$. Unfortunately, the country's communication network is outdated, so your navigation system does not always have a signal. However, the road network forms a weighted directed acyclic graph where the weight of each edge represents the time required to traverse it, and every city has a path to the capital city $$$t$$$ via the road network.

Upon arriving at any city other than $$$t$$$, you choose the next road according to the following rules:

- If there is a signal, the navigation system randomly selects one of the shortest paths from the current city to $$$t$$$ with equal probability, and directs you to take the first edge of that path;

- If there is no signal, you randomly select one of the city's outgoing edges with equal probability.

Consequently, in cities with a signal, the probability of selecting a specific outgoing edge is proportional to the number of shortest paths that begin with that edge; the probabilities of selecting different outgoing edges are not necessarily equal. A new choice is made after traversing each edge to reach the next city. All random choices are independent, and the journey ends immediately upon reaching the capital city $$$t$$$.

You want to determine, for each starting city $$$s$$$, the expected total time required to reach the capital city $$$t$$$, modulo $$$998244353$$$.

## Input

The first line contains three integers $$$n,~m,~t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le n \le 2 \times 10^5$$$, $$$0 \le m \le 4 \times 10^5$$$), representing the number of cities, the number of roads, and the ID of the capital city, respectively.

The second line contains a binary string of length $$$n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th character is $$$1$$$ if city $$$i$$$ has a signal, and $$$0$$$ otherwise. The state of city $$$t$$$ does not affect the solution to the problem.

The next $$$m$$$ lines each contain three integers $$$u,~v,~w$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$, $$$1 \le w \le 10^9$$$), representing a road from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$ with a travel time of $$$w$$$.

The graph is guaranteed to be a directed acyclic graph; there is at most one directed edge between any pair of vertices; and $$$t$$$ is the only vertex in the graph with no outgoing edges. The number of shortest paths from any vertex to $$$t$$$ is not divisible by $$$998244353$$$.

## Output

Output $$$n$$$ integers. The $$$s$$$-th integer represents the expected total travel time from city $$$s$$$ to city $$$t$$$, modulo $$$998244353$$$.

More precisely, if the expected value is expressed as an irreducible fraction $$$p/q$$$, output $$$p\cdot q^{-1}\bmod 998244353$$$, where $$$q^{-1}$$$ is the modular multiplicative inverse of $$$q$$$. It is guaranteed that this inverse exists.

## Note

In the first example, the three shortest paths from $$$1$$$ to $$$5$$$ are $$$1\to2\to5$$$, $$$1\to2\to4\to5$$$, and $$$1\to3\to5$$$. Therefore, at city $$$1$$$, the navigation system directs you to city $$$2$$$ with probability $$$2/3$$$ and to city $$$3$$$ with probability $$$1/3$$$—not by choosing each with a probability of $$$1/2$$$.

City $$$3$$$ has no signal, so its two outgoing edges are chosen with equal probability. The expected remaining time to reach the destination from there is $$$(2+3)/2 = 5/2$$$; the expected time starting from city $$$2$$$ is $$$2$$$. Thus, the expected time starting from city $$$1$$$ is $$$\frac23(1+2)+\frac13(1+\frac52)=\frac{19}{6}$$$, which is $$$166374062$$$ after modulo $$$998244353$$$.

In the second example, the two outgoing edges from city $$$4$$$ are chosen with equal probability. The navigation system resumes operation upon reaching city $$$1$$$ or $$$3$$$.
content.title: Keep on the Right Track

# Logging Compression

A system contains $$$n$$$ types of programs, indexed from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Once an instance of program type $$$k$$$ starts, it generates a log entry every $$$k$$$ seconds—specifically, at times $$$k,2k,3k,\ldots$$$ relative to its start time.

At time $$$0$$$, the system executes $$$m$$$ commands simultaneously: the $$$i$$$-th command launches one instance for each program type with an index in the range $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$. Note that if the ranges of multiple commands overlap, multiple instances of the same program type may be launched, and each instance generates logs independently.

The system records all log entries generated at times $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$. Each record contains only the index of the program type corresponding to the instance that generated the log.

Your task is to design an algorithm to compress these logs: you must assign a non-empty binary string as an identifier to all the $$$n$$$ program types, ensuring that no identifier is a prefix of another. The cost of encoding a single record is the length of the identifier assigned to the corresponding program type, and the total cost is the sum of the costs of all records. Find the minimum possible total cost.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$n,m$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 10^{10}$$$, $$$1\le m\le 10^5$$$), representing the number of types of programs and the number of commands.

Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l_i,r_i$$$ ($$$1\le l_i\le r_i\le n$$$), representing a start command.

## Output

Print a single integer: the minimum total cost.

## Note

Assume that logs are recorded in chronological order; for logs generated at the same time, the records follow a monotonically non-decreasing order based on the index of the corresponding program types.

For the first sample, the logs are $$$[1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 1, 5]$$$. An optimal assignment of identifiers is (program 1: "`0`", program 2: "`100`", program 3: "`101`", program 4: "`110`", program 5: "`111`"). The cost is $$$5 \times 1 + 2 \times 3 + 1 \times 3 + 1 \times 3 + 1 \times 3 = 20$$$.

For the second sample, the logs are $$$[1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 1, 5, 1, 2, 3, 6]$$$. An optimal assignment of identifiers is (program 1: "`0`", program 2: "`10`", program 3: "`1100`", program 4: "`1101`", program 5: "`1110`", program 6: "`1111`"). The cost is $$$6 \times 1 + 3 \times 2 + 2 \times 4 + 1 \times 4 + 1 \times 4 + 1 \times 4 = 32$$$.
content.title: Logging Compression

# Median Equals X

You are given an integer sequence $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ of length $$$n$$$, and an integer $$$x$$$.

Define a subsequence of the sequence as follows: for any non-empty set of indices $$$\{i_1,i_2,\cdots,i_m\}\ (i_1 \lt i_2 \lt \cdots \lt i_m)$$$ chosen from $$$1,\ldots,n$$$, taking $$$a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_m}$$$ in their original order is a subsequence. Define its median as follows: sort the $$$m$$$ chosen values into $$$v_1\le v_2\le\cdots\le v_m$$$, then:

- if $$$m$$$ is odd, the median is the middle value $$$v_{(m+1)/2}$$$;

- if $$$m$$$ is even, the median is the average of the two middle values, $$$\dfrac{v_{m/2}+v_{m/2+1}}{2}$$$ (this average need not be an integer, but the problem only cares whether it is exactly equal to $$$x$$$).

Find the number of subsequences whose median is exactly $$$x$$$. Since this number can be very large, output it modulo $$$998244353$$$.

Note: even if two different index sets happen to pick out the exact same multiset of values (possible since the sequence may contain repeated numbers), they are still counted as two distinct subsequences. It is the index set itself, not the multiset of chosen values, that distinguishes subsequences. The empty index set is not a subsequence and is never counted.

## Input

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t\le 10^4$$$).

For each testcase:

- The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$x$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 2\times 10^5,~-10^9\le x\le 10^9$$$), representing the length of the sequence $$$a$$$ and the target median value.

To enhance the suspense and spectator appeal of the contest, the CCPC has introduced a new format featuring a "dynamic scoreboard/balloon-awarding" system. # The Secret of Fats

Triglycerides are the main components of animal and plant fats, acting as essential substances for energy storage in the human body. Chemically, all triglycerides are formed by combining one glycerol molecule with three fatty acid molecules.

The physical and chemical properties of fats mainly depend on their connected fatty acid chains. Based on the structure of these chains, we can classify fats into two main categories: saturated fat and unsaturated fat.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/857bbe85e3782eb66094799ad4c2491935f73f9b.png)

If we know the total number of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O) atoms in a triglyceride molecule, we can directly use simple mathematical rules to determine whether it is a saturated or unsaturated fat without needing specialized laboratory instruments.

For a triglyceride completely devoid of carbon-carbon double bonds (i.e., a saturated fat). Derived from the chemical degree of unsaturation formula, the number of carbon atoms ($$$c$$$) and hydrogen atoms ($$$h$$$) of a saturated triglyceride must strictly satisfy the following linear relationship: $$$$$$ h = 2c - 4 $$$$$$ If the number of hydrogen atoms is less than this standard (i.e., $$$h \lt 2c - 4$$$), it indicates the presence of extra carbon-carbon double bonds in the carbon chain, meaning it is an unsaturated fat.

(Note: This problem guarantees that all input test data represents valid triglyceride molecules, and the number of oxygen atoms ($$$o$$$) will always be 6.)

Now, please write a program that reads the C, H, and O atomic counts of several compounds to classify them accordingly.

## Input

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$. The description of the test cases follows.

The only line of each test case contains three non-negative integers $$$c$$$, $$$h$$$, and $$$o$$$, representing the number of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms in the compound, respectively.

- $$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$

- $$$6 \le c \le 150$$$

- $$$8 \le h \le 2\times c - 4$$$, and $$$h$$$ is even.

- $$$o$$$ is guaranteed to be $$$6$$$, and the data is guaranteed to conform to the chemical rules of a valid triglyceride.

## Output

For each test case, output a single line containing the classification result of the compound:

- If it is a saturated fat, output the string `Saturated`.

- If it is an unsaturated fat, output the string `Unsaturated`.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

- Test Case 1: Carbon is 51, hydrogen is 98, and oxygen is 6. It satisfies the saturated fat condition because $$$2\times51-4=98$$$. This compound is Tripalmitin; output `Saturated`.

- Test Case 2: Carbon is 57, hydrogen is 104, and oxygen is 6. The saturated upper limit is $$$2\times57-4=110$$$. Because $$$104 \lt 110$$$, this is an unsaturated fat (Triolein, containing 3 double bonds); output `Unsaturated`.

- Test Case 3: Carbon is 55, hydrogen is 102, and oxygen is 6. The saturated upper limit is $$$2\times55-4=106$$$. Because $$$102 \lt 106$$$, it contains extra double bonds and is an unsaturated fat; output `Unsaturated`.

# Magical Girl and White Rabbits

Madoka was originally an ordinary student who went to school happily every day. However, one day she was suddenly persuaded to become a magical girl, and thus began her endless battles against enemies to protect the world.

The transportation network of this world is shaped like a complete $$$k$$$-ary tree with $$$l$$$ levels. Her base is located in Central City, which is located at the root node (level $$$1$$$), and all enemies lurk at the leaves (level $$$l$$$). Every non-leaf node has exactly $$$k$$$ children, which are ordered from left to right as its $$$1$$$-st, $$$2$$$-nd, $$$\dots$$$, $$$k$$$-th child, exactly as they are drawn in the picture below. Given $$$k$$$ and $$$l$$$, we can determine the total number of nodes in the tree (denoted $$$S$$$), which is at most $$$10^6$$$. Below is an example transportation network with $$$k = 3$$$ and $$$l = 4$$$, where $$$S=40$$$:

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/703283f7724c5649755c9157c5e187a78427fdb5.png)

Over time, Madoka has already completed $$$n$$$ enemy extermination missions sequentially. For each mission, she started her journey from Central City.

However, the enemies are not the only threat. There exists a special kind of mysterious "white rabbit" in this world that Madoka finds extremely annoying and difficult to deal with. To conserve her precious magical energy for the actual battles, Madoka actively chooses which enemy to hunt based on the safest route. She evaluates the routes to all leaves and always selects a root-to-leaf path that contains the minimum total number of white rabbits along the way.

Several different paths may share this minimum total, so Madoka fixes her route in the following deterministic way. She walks down from the root one node at a time. Standing at a non-leaf node $$$v$$$, she looks at every child $$$c$$$ of $$$v$$$ that keeps her on a path of the minimum total (that is, the number of white rabbits on the road from $$$v$$$ to $$$c$$$, plus the minimum number of white rabbits on a path from $$$c$$$ down to a leaf of $$$c$$$'s subtree, is as small as possible among all children of $$$v$$$), and she always steps into the leftmost such child, that is, the one with the smallest index among them. She repeats this until she arrives at a leaf.

Unfortunately, these white rabbits have a strange affinity for magical girls and are strongly attracted to Madoka's magical trail. After she completes the $$$i$$$-th mission, her residual magic instantly triggers a rapid multiplication of the creatures. Specifically, on every single road segment that Madoka just traveled across during that mission, the number of white rabbits permanently occupying that road increases by $$$w_i$$$. (Initially, the world was peaceful, and there were $$$0$$$ white rabbits on all roads.)

As the missions pile up, the network becomes increasingly congested with these white rabbits. Madoka needs to know how bad the situation has eventually become. Determine the total number of white rabbits Madoka will inevitably encounter on her chosen path during her NEXT ($$$n+1$$$)-th extermination mission.

## Input

The first line contains three integers $$$k$$$, $$$l$$$, and $$$n$$$, representing the branching factor of the tree, the number of levels, and the number of completed missions.

The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n$$$, representing the sequence of values by which the white rabbits increase on the traveled road segments after each mission.

- $$$1 \leq k \leq 10^6$$$

- $$$2 \leq l \leq 1000$$$

- $$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^5$$$

- $$$1 \leq w_i \leq 10^9$$$

- The total number of nodes in the tree does not exceed $$$10^6$$$.

## Output

Output a single integer representing the total number of white rabbits on the path Madoka will choose during her NEXT ($$$n+1$$$)-th mission.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

The tree has $$$4$$$ leaves, numbered $$$1$$$ to $$$4$$$ from left to right; leaves $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$ belong to the root's $$$1$$$-st child, leaves $$$3$$$ and $$$4$$$ to its $$$2$$$-nd child. Over the five missions Madoka visited leaves $$$1$$$, $$$3$$$, $$$2$$$, $$$4$$$, $$$1$$$.

The first two missions are the ones that use the tie-breaking rule. In mission $$$1$$$, every road was still empty, so all four routes tied; she went into the left child at the root and again at the next node, reaching leaf $$$1$$$. In mission $$$2$$$, the four routes cost $$$2$$$, $$$1$$$, $$$0$$$, $$$0$$$: at the root the $$$2$$$-nd child was strictly better, and there its two leaves tied at $$$0$$$, so she took the leftmost of them, leaf $$$3$$$. In the remaining three missions, the route with the fewest white rabbits was unique: leaf $$$2$$$ at cost $$$1$$$, then leaf $$$4$$$ at cost $$$2$$$, then leaf $$$1$$$ at cost $$$5$$$.

After these $$$5$$$ missions, the four routes cost $$$15$$$, $$$12$$$, $$$8$$$ and $$$10$$$, respectively. Thus, for her next mission, Madoka takes the path to leaf $$$3$$$ and will inevitably encounter exactly $$$8$$$ white rabbits.
content.title: Magical Girl and White Rabbits

# Listen to the Music

Yuki likes listening to music. She has $$$n$$$ favorite songs, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$.

She created two playlists, and each playlist contains each of these $$$n$$$ songs exactly once. In the first playlist, the $$$i$$$-th song is song $$$a_i$$$. In the second playlist, the $$$i$$$-th song is song $$$b_i$$$.

Whenever Yuki wants to listen to music, she chooses one of the two playlists and starts playing it from the first song. She may stop after any song finishes, but she will never stop in the middle of a song. In other words, each time she listens to music, she chooses one of the two playlists and listens to a non-empty prefix of it.

A year has passed, and Yuki's music system reports that song $$$i$$$ was listened to exactly $$$c_i$$$ times in total. However, Yuki suspects that this statistic may be incorrect. Please determine whether there exists some possible listening history such that, for every song $$$i$$$, the total number of times song $$$i$$$ was listened to is exactly $$$c_i$$$. Note that Yuki may not have listened to any music at all last year.

## Input

The first line contains a positive integer $$$n$$$, the number of Yuki's favorite songs.

The second line contains $$$n$$$ positive integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$, representing the order of the songs in the first playlist.

The third line contains $$$n$$$ positive integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$, representing the order of the songs in the second playlist.

The fourth line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n$$$, where $$$c_i$$$ is the total number of times song $$$i$$$ was listened to.

- $$$1 \leq n \leq 5000$$$

- Both $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are permutations of $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$.

- $$$0 \leq c_i \leq 10^9$$$

## Output

If there exists a possible listening history such that the number of times each song was listened to matches the reported statistics, output `Yes`. Otherwise, output `No`.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

Consider the playlists $$$a = [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]$$$ and $$$b = [3, 1, 2, 5, 4]$$$. Suppose Yuki listens to four prefixes as follows:

- The first $$$2$$$ songs of the first playlist, so songs $$$2$$$ and $$$4$$$ are listened to once.

- The first $$$3$$$ songs of the first playlist, so songs $$$2, 4$$$ and $$$1$$$ are listened to once.

- The first $$$4$$$ songs of the first playlist, so songs $$$2, 4, 1$$$ and $$$3$$$ are listened to once.

- The first $$$2$$$ songs of the second playlist, so songs $$$3$$$ and $$$1$$$ are listened to once.

Then the total listening counts are exactly $$$[3, 3, 2, 3, 0]$$$, which matches the reported statistics. Hence, the answer is `Yes`.

# Escape Route

In a tourist archipelago consisting of $$$n$$$ islands, there are $$$m$$$ bidirectional bridges connecting them. The islands are numbered $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th bridge connects islands $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$, and it takes $$$t_i$$$ minutes to cross. Furthermore, each bridge has a height $$$h_i$$$, representing its height above sea level in centimeters.

An unprecedented natural disaster has struck the archipelago, causing the sea level to rise at a rate of $$$1$$$ centimeter per minute. A bridge $$$i$$$ becomes unusable exactly $$$h_i$$$ minutes after the disaster begins. To ensure safety, a vehicle can only cross bridge $$$i$$$ if the entire traversal completes before the bridge is submerged. Specifically, if a vehicle starts crossing bridge $$$i$$$ at time $$$T$$$, it must arrive at the other end by time $$$T + t_i$$$, and this arrival time must satisfy $$$T + t_i \le h_i$$$.

Island $$$1$$$ serves as the evacuation center. Residents on each island are intelligent; they will choose a route that allows them to reach island $$$1$$$ safely before any bridge they cross becomes submerged. If no such path exists, they will remain on their current island to await rescue.

Given this scenario, for each island $$$k$$$ (where $$$k \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$$$), determine if the residents on island $$$k$$$ can safely reach island $$$1$$$.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$, representing the number of islands and the number of bridges, respectively.

Followed by $$$m$$$ lines, the $$$i$$$-th of which contains four integers $$$u_i, v_i, t_i, h_i$$$, representing a bridge connecting islands $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ with travel time $$$t_i$$$ and height $$$h_i$$$.

- $$$1\leq n\leq 10^5$$$

- $$$1\leq m\leq 3\times 10^5$$$

- $$$1\leq u_i, v_i \leq n, u_i\neq v_i$$$

- $$$1\leq t_i \leq h_i \leq 10^9$$$

## Output

Output a single string of length $$$n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th character of the string should be '`1`' if the residents of island $$$i$$$ can safely reach island $$$1$$$, and '`0`' otherwise.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

Residents of island $$$1$$$ are already at island $$$1$$$. Residents of island $$$3$$$ can safely cross the first bridge and arrive at island $$$1$$$ at time $$$2$$$. However, residents of island $$$2$$$ must first cross the second bridge to reach island $$$3$$$ at time $$$3$$$; if they then attempt to cross the first bridge, they will get stuck in the middle at time $$$4$$$, exactly when the bridge becomes unusable since $$$h_1=4$$$. Therefore, the residents of island $$$2$$$ cannot safely reach island $$$1$$$.

# The Graduation Photo Lineup

Class leader A-Ming is arranging the $$$n$$$ students of his class into a single row to take a graduation photo. The $$$n$$$ students all have distinct heights, and A-Ming holds a roster listing the real height of every student.

The students were already standing in some order. For fun, A-Ming handed each student a slip of paper and asked everyone to look to their right and compute one number: how many of the people standing behind them (i.e. to the right in the row) are shorter than they are? Everyone wrote down their number and handed the slip back. The slips were originally collected in left-to-right order of the row (the first slip belongs to the student standing first, and so on).

Then a sudden gust of wind scattered all the slips on the ground! A-Ming gathered them back up, but their order was completely lost, leaving only an unordered collection of numbers $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$$$.

The photographer is about to arrive and everyone has run off to play. A-Ming is left holding only the height roster and the shuffled pile of slips.

Help A-Ming decide: is it possible to reconstruct at least one valid standing order consistent with the numbers on the slips? If so, to make the picture look as harmonious as possible, output the lexicographically smallest height arrangement among all valid orders (placing shorter students as far toward the front as possible). If the numbers cannot fit together at all, output `-1`.

## Input

The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$, representing the number of students.

The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n$$$, representing the real heights of the students.

The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$$$, representing the shuffled collection of numbers written on the slips.

- $$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^5$$$

- $$$1 \leq h_i \leq 10^9$$$, and all $$$h_i$$$ are distinct.

- $$$0 \leq s_i \lt n$$$

## Output

If a valid standing order exists, output a single line of $$$n$$$ integers: the lexicographically smallest valid sequence of heights, separated by single spaces.

If no valid standing order exists, output a single line containing `-1`.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

The slips form the multiset $$$\{0, 0, 1\}$$$. Two standing orders are consistent with it: heights $$$[10, 30, 20]$$$ (slip values $$$0, 1, 0$$$) and $$$[20, 10, 30]$$$ (slip values $$$1, 0, 0$$$). The first is lexicographically smaller, so the answer is $$$10\ 30\ 20$$$.

Explanation for Sample 2

With two students, the person standing last has nobody to their right, so one slip must read $$$0$$$. Both slips read $$$1$$$, which is impossible, so the answer is $$$-1$$$.

# Marks

There is a circular track with $$$b$$$ equally spaced positions, numbered $$$0, 1, \dots, b-1$$$ clockwise. Adjacent positions are $$$1$$$ unit apart, so the whole circle measures $$$b$$$ units.

A marker starts at position $$$0$$$ and, at every step, advances by a fixed $$$a$$$ positions clockwise (wrapping back to $$$0$$$ after position $$$b-1$$$). It successively stops at $$$$$$p_k = (a \cdot k) \bmod b, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1,$$$$$$ leaving a mark at each stop, for a total of $$$n$$$ marks. It is guaranteed that $$$\gcd(a, b) = 1$$$$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ and $$$n \leq b$$$, so these $$$n$$$ marks are pairwise distinct.

These $$$n$$$ marks divide the circle into $$$n$$$ arcs. The length of an arc is the number of units it spans (every arc length is a positive integer, and the lengths sum to $$$b$$$).

How many distinct arc-length values are there? For each value, what is it, and how many times does it occur?

$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$$$$\gcd(a, b) = c$$$ means that $$$c$$$ is the largest positive integer such that $$$c$$$ divides both $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.

## Input

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$. The description of the test cases follows.

The only line of each test case contains three integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$n$$$, representing the parameters of this test case.

- $$$1 \leq t \leq 30$$$

- $$$1 \leq a \lt b \leq 10^{18}$$$

- $$$\gcd(a, b) = 1$$$

- $$$2 \leq n \leq b$$$

## Output

For each test case, first output the number of distinct arc-length values, $$$d$$$.

Followed by $$$d$$$ lines, output $$$2$$$ integers $$$s$$$ and $$$c$$$ for each of which, representing that exactly $$$c$$$ arcs have length $$$s$$$.

For each test case, output these lines in increasing order of $$$s$$$.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

The marks are $$$\{0, 7, 2, 9, 4, 11, 6\}$$$, which, when sorted, are $$$0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11$$$. The consecutive arc lengths are $$$2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1$$$, so length $$$1$$$ occurs $$$2$$$ times and length $$$2$$$ occurs $$$5$$$ times.

# Subwords

You have a grammar with the start symbol $$$S$$$, a set of variables $$$V$$$, a set of terminal symbols $$$T$$$, and a set of rules $$$P$$$. Every upper-case letter is a variable, so $$$V=\{A,\dots,Z\}$$$, and every lower-case letter is a terminal symbol, so $$$T=\{a,\dots,z\}$$$. A rule is of the form $$$A\to \alpha$$$, where $$$A\in V$$$ is a variable and $$$\alpha$$$ is a string consisting of variables and terminal symbols. The grammar never contains chain rules of the form $$$A\to B$$$, where the right side consists of a single variable. Rules of the form $$$A\to b$$$ are possible, where the right side consists of a single terminal.

A word can be derived by starting with $$$\alpha=S$$$ and then repeatedly choosing some variable $$$X$$$ in $$$\alpha$$$, some rule $$$X\to\beta$$$, and then replacing one $$$X$$$ in $$$\alpha$$$ with $$$\beta$$$. To be precise, if $$$\alpha=\alpha'X\alpha"$$$ and we have a rule $$$X\to\beta$$$, then we can replace $$$\alpha$$$ with $$$\alpha'\beta\alpha"$$$, and we write $$$\alpha\Rightarrow \alpha'\beta\alpha"$$$.

Here is a complete example. The grammar has the rules $$$$$$ S\to SA,\ \ \ S\to b,\ \ \ A\to bS,\ \ \ A\to a. $$$$$$ Then we can derive the word $$$bbb$$$ in four steps: $$$$$$ S\Rightarrow SA\Rightarrow bA\Rightarrow bbS\Rightarrow bbb. $$$$$$

On the other hand, the word $$$aaa$$$ cannot be derived.

Your task is to answer the following question for a grammar $$$G$$$ and a word $$$w$$$ (consisting of terminal symbols):

- Can you add zero or more terminal symbols at the beginning of $$$w$$$ and zero or more terminal symbols at the end of $$$w$$$ such that the resulting word $$$uwv$$$ can be derived by $$$G$$$?

## Input

The first line contains an integer $$$k$$$, representing the number of rules.

Followed by $$$k$$$ lines, each of which contains one rule. A rule is encoded by its left side, followed by ->, and then followed by its right side.

The last line contains the word $$$w$$$, representing the input word of the question.

- $$$1\leq k\leq 25$$$

- The left side of every rule is an upper-case letter.

- The right side of every rule is a string of upper-case and lower-case letters. Moreover, it is either a string of length at least $$$2$$$ or a single lower-case letter.

- The total length of the right sides of all rules is at most $$$100$$$.

- The length of $$$w$$$ is at least $$$1$$$ and at most $$$400$$$, and $$$w$$$ consists of lower-case letters.

## Output

Output a single line containing `Yes` or `No` that answers the question.

4
S -> SA
S -> b
A -> bS
A -> a
bbb

# Park of Three

The Park of Three is a famous landmark in the Kingdom of Three. It contains $$$n$$$ magical pillars connected by $$$m$$$ magical connections. The pillars are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th connection links pillar $$$u_i$$$ and pillar $$$v_i$$$, and all connections are bidirectional.

Believing that the number three holds protective power against evil forces, the park's architects ensured that every pillar is incident to exactly three connections. Note that a connection may link a pillar to itself. In such cases, the self-loop counts twice toward the number of pillar's incident connections.

Triangles formed by the pillars are the source of their protective power. Historically, these triangles successfully repelled evil forces hundreds of years ago. To assess the network's true resilience, you must determine its structural vulnerability.

Formally, three distinct pillars $$$i, j, k$$$ form a triangle if the connections $$$(i, j)$$$, $$$(j, k)$$$, and $$$(k, i)$$$ all exist. When a pillar is destroyed, all connections incident to it are removed. The strength of the park is defined as the minimum number $$$s$$$ such that destroying $$$s$$$ specific pillars eliminates all triangles. Please determine the strength $$$s$$$ and output the indices of $$$s$$$ pillars such that there will be no triangles after destroying them.

## Input

The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$, representing the number of magical pillars in the park.

Followed by $$$m = \frac{3n}{2}$$$ lines, the $$$i$$$-th of which contains two integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$, representing the endpoints of the $$$i$$$-th magical connection.

- $$$4 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^5$$$, and $$$n$$$ is even.

- $$$1 \leq u_i, v_i \leq n$$$ for all $$$1 \leq i \leq m$$$.

- The network of magical connections may contain self-loops and multiple connections between the same pair of pillars.

- Each pillar is incident to exactly $$$3$$$ connections, where each self-loop is counted twice toward this total.

## Output

On the first line, output the integer $$$s$$$.

On the second line, output $$$s$$$ distinct integers representing the indices of the pillars to be destroyed. After removing these pillars and all incident connections, no triangles should remain.

If multiple solutions exist, output any of them. The indices may be printed in any order.

## Note

Explanation for Sample 1

The network of connections is shown in the figure below. There are $$$4$$$ triangles formed by the pillars: $$$(1, 2, 3)$$$, $$$(1, 2, 4)$$$, $$$(1, 3, 4)$$$, and $$$(2, 3, 4)$$$. After destroying pillars $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$, no triangle remains in the network. Any subset of $$$\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$$ of size 2 is also a valid solution.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/1fa651a00c758c48decdfb26342233053c9a80c3.png)

# A Bit of History

Kyrgyzstan has been taking part in ICPC competitions since 1996, when the North-Eastern European Regional Contest (NEERC) was organized.

In the 2003-2004 season, the team from Kyrgyzstan reached the ICPC World Finals for the first time, and in 2005 the first ICPC regional championship was held in Kyrgyzstan.

Since then, the regional championship has been held every year.

In 2019, due to the increase in the number of participants, an additional qualification stage was introduced — but due to COVID restrictions, it was not held in 2020 and 2021.

However, all of this is true for student teams — school teams from Kyrgyzstan that wanted to participate in the VKOSHP finals had to qualify every year through the general online selection.

And now, in 2026, the situation for school teams has finally changed — now, in parallel with the student team championship in Kyrgyzstan, which is a qualifier for the NERC Finals, a school team championship is also held, which is a qualifier for VKOSHP.

As in the case of student teams, school teams first need to pass a qualification stage, and based on its results the best teams will advance to the main stage of the championship.

The author of this problem decided that this event is a good basis for a problem.

For a given year $$$Y$$$, output all team competitions that were held or will be held in Kyrgyzstan in that year.

## Input

The only line contains an integer $$$Y$$$ $$$(2005 \le Y \le 2026)$$$ — the year of the competitions.

## Output

In the first line, output an integer $$$k$$$ — the number of team competitions held (or to be held) in year $$$Y$$$ in Kyrgyzstan.

In the next $$$k$$$ lines, output one competition per line (in any order):

- if in year $$$Y$$$ there was/will be a student team championship — output `ICPC Regional`;

- if in year $$$Y$$$ there was/will be a qualification for the student championship — output `ICPC Qual`;

- if in year $$$Y$$$ there was/will be a school team championship — output `School Regional`;

- if in year $$$Y$$$ there was/will be a qualification for the school championship — output `School Qual`.

The lines may be output in any order.

## Note

In the first example ($$$Y = 2026$$$), for the first time in history, all four competitions are held in the same year at once: the ICPC student championship, its qualification, as well as the newly introduced school championship and its qualification.

In the second example ($$$Y = 2019$$$), this is the first year when, in addition to the ICPC student regional championship, its qualification was also held.

In the third example ($$$Y = 2021$$$), due to COVID restrictions, the qualification stage for the student championship was not held again (as in 2020), so only the ICPC regional championship itself took place.

In the fourth example ($$$Y = 2007$$$), we go back to 2007, when only the ICPC student regional championship was held, without any qualifications.

# Chatbot on a Calculator

Did you know that in the past, even calculators were programmed in computer science classes?

The author of this problem personally learned about this from their parents, who did something similar in the late 1980s.

In 2026, the main trend is communicating with various LLM models in chat mode (and not only that).

But is it possible to communicate in a similar way with a chatbot programmed on a calculator?

It is possible if we consider some digits to be similar to letters of the Latin alphabet:

- digit 0 is similar to O;

- digit 1 is similar to I;

- digit 5 is similar to S;

- digit 8 is similar to B.

And if you turn the calculator upside down, you can see two more correspondences:

- digit 3 is similar to an upside-down E;

- digit 7 is similar to an upside-down L.

We will call a number $$$X$$$ a "word" if all of its digits are similar to letters:

- number 8015 looks like the word "BOIS";

- number 5337 does not look like a word, but when turned upside down it looks like "LEES";

- number 123 does not look like a word, since digit 2 is not similar to any letter;

- number 0158 is not a valid number, since it starts with a leading zero.

Your task is to determine the number of word-like numbers in the interval $$$[0; N]$$$.

## Input

The only line contains one integer $$$N$$$ $$$(0 \le N \le 123456)$$$ — the upper bound of the interval $$$[0; N]$$$.

## Output

Print two integers $$$C_1$$$ and $$$C_2$$$ separated by a space:

- $$$C_1$$$ — the number of numbers in the interval $$$[0; N]$$$ that look like a word in the normal orientation;

- $$$C_2$$$ — the number of numbers in the interval $$$[0; N]$$$ that look like a word in the turned upside down orientation.

## Note

Example 1.

In the normal orientation, the following numbers look like words:

- $$$0, 1, 5, 8$$$;

- $$$10, 11, 15, 18$$$.

There are $$$8$$$ such numbers in the interval $$$[0; 34]$$$.

In the turned upside down orientation, the following numbers look like words:

- $$$0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8$$$;

- $$$10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18$$$;

- $$$30, 31, 33$$$.

There are $$$15$$$ such numbers in the interval $$$[0; 34]$$$.

Example 2.

This test is an additional opportunity to check that your counting is performed correctly.

Example 3.

This test checks that your counting is performed efficiently enough (the bound $$$N$$$ takes its maximum possible value).

# Uniform Change

A cashier has an infinite number of banknotes with denominations $$$1, 2, \ldots, K$$$.

The cashier prefers the stacks of banknotes to end uniformly:

- Suppose the cashier gives change as $$$C_1$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$1$$$, $$$C_2$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$2$$$, ..., $$$C_K$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$K$$$.

- The cashier wants the maximum value among $$$C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_K$$$ to be as small as possible.

Help the cashier — find any way to give $$$N$$$ units of change uniformly.

## Input

The only line contains two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$K$$$ separated by a space ($$$1 \le N \le 10^{18}$$$; $$$1 \le K \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the amount of change and the number of different available denominations.

## Output

Print $$$K$$$ integers $$$C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_K$$$ ($$$0 \le C_i \le N$$$) separated by spaces — the number of banknotes of denomination $$$i$$$ in a uniform change of $$$N$$$.

The answer must satisfy the following conditions:

- $$$\sum_{i=1}^{K} C_i \cdot i = N$$$ — exactly $$$N$$$ units of change are given;

- $$$\max(C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_K)$$$ is minimal among all ways to give change of size $$$N$$$ using denominations from $$$1$$$ to $$$K$$$.

If there are multiple answers satisfying the conditions, print any of them.

## Note

In the first example, the cashier gave:

- $$$C_1 = 2$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$1$$$;

- $$$C_2 = 1$$$ banknote of denomination $$$2$$$;

- $$$C_3 = 2$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$3$$$.

In total, the cashier gave $$$C_1 \cdot 1 + C_2 \cdot 2 + C_3 \cdot 3 = 10$$$ units.

In the second example, the cashier gave:

- $$$1$$$ banknote of denomination $$$1$$$;

- $$$3$$$ banknotes each of denominations $$$2, 3, 4, 5, 6$$$;

- $$$0$$$ banknotes of denomination $$$7$$$.

In total, the cashier gave $$$1 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) + 0 \cdot 7 = 61$$$ units.

Note that this is only one possible answer with $$$\max(C_1, \ldots, C_7) = 3$$$. It can be shown that there is no answer where $$$\max(C_1, \ldots, C_7)$$$ is less than $$$3$$$.

# Median for Every Prefix!

You are given a permutation $$$P$$$ of length $$$N$$$.

For each prefix of this permutation, you need to compute its median.

## Input

The first line contains one integer $$$N$$$ $$$(1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5)$$$ — the length of the permutation.

The second line contains $$$N$$$ integers $$$P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_N$$$ $$$(1 \le P_i \le N)$$$ separated by spaces — the elements of the permutation.

It is guaranteed that all values $$$P_i$$$ are distinct.

## Output

Print $$$N$$$ integers $$$M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_N$$$ separated by spaces, where $$$M_i$$$ is the doubled median of the elements $$$P_1, \ldots, P_i$$$ (that is, the median of the first $$$i$$$ elements of the permutation multiplied by $$$2$$$).

## Note

The median of a set of $$$k$$$ numbers sorted in nondecreasing order as $$$a_1 \le a_2 \le \ldots \le a_k$$$ is defined as:

- if $$$k$$$ is odd — the value $$$a_{(k+1)/2}$$$;

- if $$$k$$$ is even — the arithmetic mean of the values $$$a_{k/2}$$$ and $$$a_{k/2+1}$$$, that is, $$$\dfrac{a_{k/2} + a_{k/2+1}}{2}$$$.

Since the median for even $$$k$$$ may not be an integer, you should output its doubled value — it is always an integer.

Let us consider the first example step by step. At each step $$$i$$$, we consider the prefix of the first $$$i$$$ elements of the permutation sorted in nondecreasing order, and compute its doubled median $$$M_i$$$:

- $$$i = 1$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[5]$$$, the median is $$$5$$$, $$$M_1 = 2 \cdot 5 = 10$$$.

- $$$i = 2$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[2, 5]$$$, the median is $$$(2+5)/2$$$, $$$M_2 = 2 + 5 = 7$$$.

- $$$i = 3$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[1, 2, 5]$$$, the median is $$$2$$$, $$$M_3 = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$$$.

- $$$i = 4$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[1, 2, 4, 5]$$$, the median is $$$(2+4)/2$$$, $$$M_4 = 2 + 4 = 6$$$.

- $$$i = 5$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[1, 2, 4, 5, 7]$$$, the median is $$$4$$$, $$$M_5 = 2 \cdot 4 = 8$$$.

- $$$i = 6$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]$$$, the median is $$$(4+5)/2$$$, $$$M_6 = 4 + 5 = 9$$$.

- $$$i = 7$$$: sorted prefix — $$$[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]$$$, the median is $$$4$$$, $$$M_7 = 2 \cdot 4 = 8$$$.
content.title: Median for Every Prefix!

# Borders

In the country of Logoria there are $$$N$$$ independent towns. Each town is located at a point of the plane with integer coordinates $$$(x_i, y_i)$$$.

At first, each town forms its own community. Then an era of conflicts begins. Each conflict involves two towns $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$: after it, the communities to which towns $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ belong become a single community (it does not matter who wins the dispute). If $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ already belong to the same community, the conflict produces no change.

The territory of a community is the smallest convex region that contains all of its towns. The boundary of this territory is known as the convex hull of its points.

After each conflict, determine twice the area of the territory of the resulting community. If all the towns of a community lie on the same line, its area is considered to be zero. It can be shown that twice the area is always an integer.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/cce7140e72a6baed2dc1b30827f6983d8534af41.png)

Three towns forming a triangle of area $$$6$$$.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$M$$$ ($$$2 \leq N \leq 2000$$$, $$$1 \leq M \leq 100000$$$), where $$$N$$$ is the number of towns and $$$M$$$ is the number of conflicts.

Each of the following $$$N$$$ lines contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$-1000000 \leq x_i, y_i \leq 1000000$$$), the coordinates of the $$$i$$$-th town. The towns are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$N$$$, and all of them have distinct coordinates: $$$(x_i, y_i) \neq (x_j, y_j)$$$ for $$$i \neq j$$$.

Each of the following $$$M$$$ lines contains two integers $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ ($$$1 \leq a, b \leq N$$$), meaning that the communities containing towns $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ merge. A conflict may involve two towns that already belong to the same community.

## Output

Print $$$M$$$ lines. The $$$j$$$-th line must contain twice the area of the territory of the community that contains the towns of the $$$j$$$-th conflict, immediately after applying that conflict.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

Initially there are five independent towns: $$$\{1\}$$$, $$$\{2\}$$$, $$$\{3\}$$$, $$$\{4\}$$$ and $$$\{5\}$$$.

After the conflict between towns $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$, the resulting community has only two towns, so the answer is $$$0$$$.

The conflict between $$$2$$$ and $$$3$$$ joins $$$\{1,2\}$$$ with $$$\{3\}$$$: the three towns form a triangle of area $$$6$$$, so twice that value, $$$12$$$, is printed.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/cce7140e72a6baed2dc1b30827f6983d8534af41.png)

Community $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$ forms a triangle with twice the area equal to $$$12$$$.

The conflict between $$$4$$$ and $$$5$$$ forms a community of two towns and again produces $$$0$$$.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/9b3f3eb78bae4c8f67c0fd10f77bf99a82cddb41.png)

In the same plane, community $$$\{4,5\}$$$ is just a segment (2 towns, area 0); community $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$ is shown in gray for reference.

Finally, the conflict between $$$1$$$ and $$$4$$$ joins $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$ with $$$\{4,5\}$$$. Town $$$5 = (2,1)$$$ lies inside the rectangle formed by the other four towns and does not change the boundary; that rectangle has area $$$12$$$, so the answer is $$$24$$$.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e05ee02ddd7d74a3590310e7dbbb214348fa5f7b.png)

When the two communities (dashed lines) merge, town $$$5$$$ ends up in the interior of the new boundary (solid line).

Explanation for example 2

The first three towns lie on the same line, so as long as the community does not include town $$$4$$$ the answer is $$$0$$$; in particular, the second conflict ($$$1$$$-$$$2$$$) does not change the community, because $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$ already belonged to $$$\{1,2\}$$$. When town $$$4$$$ joins, the hull becomes the triangle with vertices $$$(0,0)$$$, $$$(2,0)$$$ and $$$(0,2)$$$, whose doubled area is $$$4$$$.

Explanation for example 3

Conflicts $$$1$$$-$$$2$$$ and $$$1$$$-$$$3$$$ form community $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$, whose boundary is triangle $$$P_1P_2P_3$$$ (twice the area: $$$24$$$).

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/3981bd4374269dc41fe76ce1d9d45c2292ec478a.png)

Community $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$ forms a triangle with twice the area equal to $$$24$$$.

Independently, conflicts $$$4$$$-$$$5$$$ and $$$4$$$-$$$6$$$ form $$$\{4,5,6\}$$$, with boundary $$$P_4P_5P_6$$$ (twice the area: $$$18$$$).

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/629ebed8101067a7c457d52c15b6c215cfe52a9c.png)

In the same plane, community $$$\{4,5,6\}$$$ forms a triangle with twice the area equal to $$$18$$$ (community $$$\{1,2,3\}$$$ is shown in gray for reference).

Conflict $$$1$$$-$$$4$$$ joins both communities. The new boundary is pentagon $$$P_1P_4P_5P_2P_6$$$, and town $$$3$$$ ends up in its interior despite having been a vertex of its own community's boundary just before the merge: this is why it is not enough to combine the two previous boundaries; the convex hull of the union must be recomputed. Twice the area of the pentagon is $$$58$$$.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/0033a356b338b24c4307644987defa6aaf4ea862.png)

When the two communities (dashed lines) merge, town $$$3$$$ stops being a vertex of the new boundary (solid line).

# MiniMax

You are given an array of $$$n$$$ integers, which may be negative, zero or positive, and a positive integer $$$k$$$.

You must answer $$$q$$$ queries. Each query gives two positions $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$. Your task is to split the subarray $$$a[l..r]$$$ into the minimum possible number of non-empty contiguous segments, such that, in each segment, the difference between its maximum element and its minimum element is less than or equal to $$$k$$$.

The segments must cover exactly the queried subarray, without overlapping and keeping the original order of the elements. A segment with a single element has difference zero.

Positions are numbered starting from $$$1$$$. The array and the value of $$$k$$$ are the same for all queries. The queries are independent and do not modify the array.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \leq n, q \leq 10^{5}$$$): the length of the array and the number of queries.

The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$-10^{9} \leq a_i \leq 10^{9}$$$).

The third line contains an integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq k \leq 10^{9}$$$).

Each of the following $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1 \leq l \leq r \leq n$$$), representing a query on $$$a[l..r]$$$.

The input contains a single test case and is read from standard input.

## Output

For each query, print on a line of standard output the minimum number of segments required, in the same order in which the queries are received.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

For $$$[1, 7]$$$, an optimal partition is $$$[1] \mid [5, 3, 2] \mid [7, 6, 4]$$$. The differences are $$$0$$$, $$$3$$$ and $$$3$$$. It is mandatory to cut between $$$1$$$ and $$$5$$$, and between $$$2$$$ and $$$7$$$, because each of those consecutive pairs has a difference greater than $$$3$$$. Therefore, at least three segments are needed.

For $$$[2, 5]$$$, an optimal partition is $$$[5, 3, 2] \mid [7]$$$. The whole subarray has difference $$$7 - 2 = 5 \gt 3$$$, so a single segment is not enough.

For $$$[3, 4]$$$, the segment $$$[3, 2]$$$ has difference $$$1$$$, so the answer is $$$1$$$.

Explanation for example 2

For $$$[1, 6]$$$, an optimal partition is $$$[-3, -1, 0] \mid [2, 2] \mid [-2]$$$. There must be a cut before the first $$$2$$$, because it cannot share a segment with $$$-3$$$, and another cut between the last $$$2$$$ and $$$-2$$$, whose difference is $$$4$$$. Those cuts are different, so at least three segments are needed.

For $$$[2, 5]$$$, the subarray $$$[-1, 0, 2, 2]$$$ has difference $$$3$$$ and fits in a single segment.

For $$$[3, 3]$$$, the subarray contains only the zero and requires one segment.

For $$$[5, 6]$$$, the values $$$2$$$ and $$$-2$$$ have difference $$$4$$$ and must be placed in separate segments.

# Firewood in Corani

The 2880 algorithms club went to Corani and is now preparing firewood for the fireplace. The little wood logs are cylindrical and stacked in the shape of a triangular pyramid: there are $$$N$$$ logs at the base, $$$N-1$$$ in the next row, and so on until a single log at the top.

Pakai came up with the idea of playing by removing logs from the base and discovered an interesting problem. Each log in an upper row rests on the two logs immediately below it. If it loses either of its two supports, it falls. This can make other logs fall in a chain reaction. Fallen logs are removed from the pile without hitting or displacing the others.

Pakai will remove $$$Q$$$ logs from the base, one by one, waiting for all the falls to finish after each removal. The positions of the base are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$N$$$, from left to right, and keep their original numbering throughout the whole process (fallen or removed logs never return to the pile).

How many logs remain in the whole pyramid after each removal?

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$Q$$$ ($$$1 \leq N \leq 10^{9}$$$; $$$1 \leq Q \leq \min(N, 2 \times 10^{5})$$$).

Each of the following $$$Q$$$ lines contains an integer $$$p_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq N$$$): the position of the base log that Pakai removes in operation $$$i$$$. All positions $$$p_i$$$ are pairwise distinct.

## Output

Print $$$Q$$$ lines. On line $$$i$$$, write the total number of logs that remain in the whole pyramid after operation $$$i$$$ (that is, after removing $$$p_i$$$ and all the falls that this removal causes).

## Note

Explanation for example 1

Initially there are $$$15$$$ logs. After removing the one at position $$$3$$$, two intact stretches of two positions each remain (positions $$$1,2$$$ and $$$4,5$$$), which support $$$3+3=6$$$ logs. After removing the one at position $$$1$$$, the left stretch is reduced to position $$$2$$$ alone and $$$1+3=4$$$ logs remain. Finally, after removing the one at position $$$5$$$, only the base logs at positions $$$2$$$ and $$$4$$$ survive, each one supporting only itself: $$$1+1=2$$$ logs.

Explanation for example 2

This case illustrates the ends of the base. Initially there are $$$21$$$ logs. After removing position $$$1$$$ (the left end), a single stretch with positions $$$2,\ldots,6$$$ survives, which supports $$$15$$$ logs. After then removing position $$$6$$$ (the right end), the stretch $$$2,\ldots,5$$$ survives, which supports $$$10$$$ logs.

# Cookies for the Feed

For an Instagram reel of icpc_umss, the team wants to bake letter-shaped cookies and use them to spell several words. Each word is prepared in one batch: all of its letters are baked at the same time, using one mold per cookie.

Each mold has a fixed letter and can be reused, but it must cool down for one full batch after each use. For example, a mold used in the first batch cannot be used in the second one, but it can be used in the third.

The words must be prepared in the given order, with no additional pauses or empty batches. At the beginning, all molds are cold. What is the minimum total number of molds that must be bought before starting?

## Input

The first line contains an integer $$$N$$$ ($$$1 \leq N \leq 1000$$$), the number of words.

Each of the following $$$N$$$ lines contains a word $$$S_i$$$ of between $$$1$$$ and $$$1000$$$ uppercase letters of the English alphabet (`A` to `Z`). Repeated letters require different molds within the same batch.

## Output

Print an integer: the minimum total number of molds needed.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

Three `A` molds, one `N`, one `L` and one `I` are bought. The first batch uses two `A` molds and the `N` mold; the second uses the third `A` mold, the `L` mold and the `I` mold. By the third batch the molds from the first batch are already cold, so the two `A` molds and the `N` mold can be reused.

Explanation for example 2

Two `C` molds, one `I` and one `P` are needed: the word `ICPC` uses the letter `C` twice in the same batch, so two different molds of that letter are required.

# Lights for the SanSiCup

Every Christmas, while decorating the hall, the kids of ICPC UMSS organize the SanSiCup. On a wall there is a panel with $$$b$$$ lights, numbered from $$$0$$$ to $$$b-1$$$, and $$$N$$$ remote controls. At the beginning all lights are off.

Each control $$$i$$$ has an associated fixed mask $$$a_i$$$: when pressed, it toggles exactly the lights $$$j$$$ such that bit $$$j$$$ of $$$a_i$$$ is one (lights that are off turn on and lights that are on turn off). The controls can be pressed in any order and as many times as desired; pressing the same control twice cancels its effect. Consequently, a configuration of lights (the subset of lights that are on) is reachable if and only if it is equal to the bitwise XOR of the masks of some subset of the original controls (the empty subset produces the configuration with all lights off).

Since the controls often get lost among the decorations, the kids want to build some additional backup controls. The effect of each new control is chosen before any loss happens, is fixed at that moment and cannot be changed afterwards; that effect must be equal to the XOR of the masks of some subset of the original controls (not of other new controls). A new control with mask $$$0$$$ is valid, although useless.

Then, up to two arbitrary controls —original or new, in any combination— may be lost. Two different controls are always considered physical and separate even if they have exactly the same mask: losing one of them does not affect the other. Once the new controls are built and the identity of the lost controls is known, the kids can freely choose, for each configuration they want to reproduce, which remaining controls to press (different subsets for different configurations are allowed).

The kids want that, no matter which up to two controls are lost, every configuration that was reachable with the $$$N$$$ original controls (without losses and without new controls) remains reachable using only the controls that survived. What is the minimum number of additional controls they need to build to guarantee this?

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$b$$$ ($$$1 \leq N \leq 100000$$$, $$$1 \leq b \leq 60$$$): the number of original controls and the number of lights on the panel.

The second line contains $$$N$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N$$$ ($$$0 \leq a_i \lt 2^b$$$), the masks of the original controls, in decimal. The lights are numbered from $$$0$$$ to $$$b-1$$$: control $$$i$$$ toggles light $$$j$$$ if and only if bit $$$j$$$ of $$$a_i$$$ is one.

Several original controls may have exactly the same mask (including mask $$$0$$$, a control that does not change any light); each one counts as an independent physical unit that can be lost separately.

## Output

Print a single integer: the minimum number of additional controls the kids must build.

## Note

Remember that:

- The effect of each new control is fixed before it is known which controls will be lost, and it must be expressible as the XOR of masks of original controls (never of other new controls).

- "Losing up to two controls" includes losing zero, one or two controls, in any combination of original and new ones.

- Two controls with the same mask are still distinct units: losing one does not imply losing the other.

Explanation for example 1

It is enough to build one additional control with mask $$$3$$$ (equivalent to pressing the controls with masks $$$2$$$ and $$$1$$$). With the six available controls, every configuration reachable with the five original ones remains reachable even if any two of them are lost.

For example, if the controls with masks $$$4$$$ and $$$2$$$ are lost, the effect of the first one can be reconstructed by pressing those with masks $$$5$$$ and $$$1$$$, and the effect of the second one by pressing those with masks $$$3$$$ and $$$1$$$.

Without building any additional control, losing the controls with masks $$$2$$$ and $$$6$$$ already makes it impossible to obtain configuration $$$2$$$.

Explanation for example 2

The three original controls are linearly independent (they form a basis) and none of them has a backup: losing any one of them already makes it impossible to reproduce its effect. An optimal choice is to build the controls with masks $$$6$$$, $$$5$$$ and $$$3$$$.

Explanation for example 3

Even if two of the three controls are lost, there is always one left that can turn the only light on or off. There is no need to build any additional control.
content.title: Lights for the SanSiCup

# Sergio's Happiest Office

Sergio runs an office with $$$m$$$ windows arranged in a row. Blind $$$j$$$ currently leaves an opening of $$$a_j$$$ centimeters and cannot be opened beyond $$$h_j$$$ centimeters.

Sergio's colleagues, Miguel and Racsó, convinced him that the team must get enough natural light: according to the wellness program, reasonable sun exposure helps maintain healthy vitamin D levels and improves the mood in the office. There are $$$n$$$ office workers in total.

Office worker $$$i$$$ receives light from all windows from $$$l_i$$$ to $$$r_i$$$, inclusive. Their light level is the sum of the openings of those blinds.

While Miguel and Racsó are at lunch, Sergio can only raise blinds. So that the change is not obvious, the building controller allows at most $$$k$$$ centimeters of total movement. He must choose non-negative integers $$$x_1, \ldots, x_m$$$ such that $$$$$$x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_m \leq k$$$$$$ and $$$$$$a_j + x_j \leq h_j$$$$$$ for each blind $$$j$$$. After the adjustment, the opening of blind $$$j$$$ will be $$$a_j + x_j$$$ centimeters. It is guaranteed that at least one adjustment satisfying all the constraints exists.

The management wants to maximize the light received by the least illuminated office worker. Print only that maximum value.

## Input

The first line contains three integers $$$m$$$, $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq m, n \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$$$, $$$0 \leq k \leq 10^{12}$$$).

The second line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$a_1, \ldots, a_m$$$ ($$$0 \leq a_j \leq 10^{9}$$$).

The third line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$h_1, \ldots, h_m$$$ ($$$a_j \leq h_j \leq 10^{9}$$$).

Each of the following $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq l_i \leq r_i \leq m$$$). Different office workers may have the same interval of windows.

## Output

Print a single integer: the maximum possible value of the minimum illumination among all office workers.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

Sergio can raise the blinds by $$$0, 2, 0, 3$$$ centimeters. The light levels of the three office workers become $$$3, 4, 4$$$. Achieving at least $$$4$$$ for all of them would require three centimeters on the first two windows and three on the fourth, a total of six centimeters; Sergio only has five.
content.title: Sergio's Happiest Office

# Racsó's Toy Train

Racsó has a toy train that he loves. It has $$$n$$$ numbered stations joined by $$$m$$$ bidirectional track segments. Initially, the train can travel from any station to any other.

Two distinct stations are well connected if, after any track segment comes loose, the train can still travel between those two stations. Only one segment comes loose at a time.

Miguel wants to make the train more reliable. For each of $$$q$$$ plans he can add two colored track segments: one between stations $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, and another between stations $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$.

For each plan, count the unordered pairs of distinct stations that satisfy the following three conditions:

- They are well connected if both new segments are added.

- They are not well connected if only the segment between $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ is added.

- They are not well connected if only the segment between $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ is added.

In each scenario, the segment that comes loose can be any of those that exist in it, including the two new ones.

The plans are independent: each one starts from Racsó's original train and no new segment is kept for the next plan.

A new segment may join the same stations as an original track or as the other proposed segment. They are different physical tracks: if one comes loose, the others keep working. The four stations of a plan do not have to be distinct.

## Input

The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$$$, $$$n - 1 \leq m \leq 3 \times 10^{5}$$$, $$$1 \leq q \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$$$).

The next $$$m$$$ lines contain two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \leq u, v \leq n$$$, $$$u \neq v$$$), the endpoints of an original segment. The train is connected and does not contain two original segments with the same endpoints.

The next $$$q$$$ lines contain four integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ ($$$1 \leq a, b, c, d \leq n$$$, $$$a \neq b$$$, $$$c \neq d$$$), describing a plan with two new segments.

## Output

Print $$$q$$$ lines. On each line, print the number of pairs corresponding to that plan. Each pair is counted only once, regardless of the order of its stations.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

In the first plan, the only pair that needs both new segments is $$$\{1,4\}$$$. With only the first one, the train depends on segment $$$3\text{-}4$$$; with only the second one, it depends on $$$1\text{-}2$$$.

In the second plan, additional copies of segments $$$1\text{-}2$$$ and $$$2\text{-}3$$$ are added. The pair $$$\{1,3\}$$$ becomes well connected only when both copies are added.

In the last plan, the pairs that satisfy the conditions are $$$\{1,4\}$$$ and $$$\{2,4\}$$$.

Explanation for example 2

The pairs are $$$\{2,4\}$$$, $$$\{2,5\}$$$, $$$\{3,4\}$$$ and $$$\{3,5\}$$$. The alternative routes of the train are allowed to pass through the same station: being well connected refers to a loose segment, not to a closed station.
content.title: Racsó's Toy Train

# Backup Ink

A print shop represents a strip of paper by a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$. Each position of the string corresponds to a cell of the strip.

To test a pattern $$$t$$$, which must be a non-empty substring of $$$s$$$, the print shop starts with all cells unpainted. Then it performs one ink application for each occurrence of $$$t$$$ in $$$s$$$.

If an occurrence starts at position $$$i$$$, its application paints all the cells of the interval $$$[i, i + |t| - 1]$$$. Applications may overlap: a cell is considered painted as long as at least one application covers it.

The print shop wants to measure what happens if an application fails. To do so, it cancels exactly one of the applications and keeps all the others. The damage of that cancellation is the number of cells that were painted and stop being painted.

A pattern is resilient if the damage is at most $$$k$$$, no matter which of its applications is cancelled.

Compute how many distinct non-empty substrings of $$$s$$$ are resilient.

The tests of different patterns and the different cancellations are considered independently. Cancelling an application does not modify the characters of $$$s$$$ nor the positions of its occurrences. The pattern does not need to paint the whole strip.

Two substrings are considered equal if they have the same length and the same characters, even if they appear at different positions.

## Input

The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$$$, $$$0 \leq k \leq n$$$): the length of the string and the maximum allowed damage.

The second line contains a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$, consisting only of lowercase letters of the English alphabet.

## Output

Print an integer: the number of distinct non-empty substrings that are resilient.

The answer may not fit in a 32-bit integer.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

The resilient patterns are `a`, `aa`, `aaa` and `aaaa`.

For example, `aaa` occurs in the intervals $$$[1,3]$$$, $$$[2,4]$$$ and $$$[3,5]$$$. When the first application is cancelled, only cell $$$1$$$ stops being painted. When the middle application is cancelled, no cell stops being painted. When the last one is cancelled, only cell $$$5$$$ stops being painted.

The pattern `aaaaa` is not resilient: it has a single occurrence and, when its application is cancelled, all five cells stop being painted.

Explanation for example 2

The resilient patterns are `a`, `b`, `aa` and `aaaa`.

The pattern `aaa` is not resilient: when the application corresponding to $$$[7,9]$$$ is cancelled, the three cells of that interval stop being painted.

On the other hand, `aaaa` occurs in $$$[1,4]$$$, $$$[2,5]$$$, $$$[11,14]$$$ and $$$[12,15]$$$. Cancelling any of those applications causes a damage of one cell.

Explanation for example 3

All distinct substrings are resilient: `a`, `b`, `c`, `ab`, `bc` and `abc`. Each of them has a single occurrence, but cancelling its application causes a damage of at most $$$3$$$.
content.title: Backup Ink

# The Single-Cut Cross

In a workshop there are $$$n$$$ cables laid out on a plane. Cable $$$i$$$ is the straight segment joining $$$A_i=(x_{i,1},y_{i,1})$$$ with $$$B_i=(x_{i,2},y_{i,2})$$$ and has a value $$$w_i$$$.

At the origin $$$O=(0,0)$$$ there is a machine with two lasers. Each laser occupies an infinite line passing through the origin. The two lines are perpendicular and can rotate together, always keeping an angle of $$$90^\circ$$$ between them.

You must choose an orientation of the machine and activate it only once. Both lasers are activated simultaneously and go through all the cables they meet, without stopping.

An orientation is valid if it satisfies the following conditions:

- Neither of the two lasers passes through an endpoint of any cable.

- No cable is intersected by both lasers.

In a valid orientation, a cable is considered cut if one of the lasers intersects its interior, that is, the segment without its endpoints. Each cut cable contributes its value $$$w_i$$$; cables that are not cut contribute nothing.

Find the maximum total value that can be obtained with a valid orientation. If there is none, print $$$-1$$$.

It is not necessary to cut all the cables, or even one. However, if both lasers intersect the same cable, the whole orientation is invalid: you cannot simply discard that cable from the score.

It is guaranteed that no cable contains the origin. Cables may cross, share endpoints or overlap; they are considered independent objects and their values are counted separately.

## Input

The first line contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^{4}$$$), the number of test cases.

For each test case:

The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$$$), the number of cables.

Each of the following $$$n$$$ lines contains five integers:

$$$$$$x_{i,1}\quad y_{i,1}\quad x_{i,2}\quad y_{i,2}\quad w_i$$$$$$

with the constraints

$$$$$$-10^{9}\le x_{i,1},y_{i,1},x_{i,2},y_{i,2}\le 10^{9},$$$$$$

$$$$$$1\le w_i\le 10^{9}.$$$$$$

The endpoints of each cable are distinct and the segment joining them does not contain $$$(0,0)$$$.

The sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \times 10^{5}$$$.

## Output

For each test case, print an integer: the maximum total value of the cut cables with a valid orientation, or $$$-1$$$ if there is no valid orientation.

## Note

Explanation for example 1

In the first case, the lines $$$y=\frac52x$$$ and $$$y=-\frac25x$$$ form a valid orientation. The second and third cables are cut, obtaining $$$7+4=11$$$. There is no valid orientation that achieves a larger value.

In the second case, the coordinate axes form a valid orientation that cuts only the first cable, obtaining $$$5$$$. Any orientation that cuts the cable of value $$$100$$$ intersects the first cable with both lasers, so it is invalid.

In the third case, the cables form the outline of a triangle that contains the origin in its interior. Every line through the origin that avoids the vertices crosses two sides. Between the two lasers there are four intersections with only three cables, so at least one of them receives two cuts. There is no valid orientation.

In the fourth case, the cable lies on the same ray that starts at the origin and passes through $$$(1,1)$$$. A line through the origin can only cut it if it also passes through its endpoints, which is forbidden. Valid orientations exist, but none of them cuts the cable; the answer is $$$0$$$.
content.title: The Single-Cut Cross
